claims.claim: As of October 10, 2026, Codie Sanchez is the founder and CEO of Contrarian Thinking, which her press release describes as a media, advisory and investment company, and the author of Main Street Millionaire and Own or Be Owned.
claims.passage: Sanchez is the founder and CEO of Contrarian Thinking, a media, advisory and investment company
claims.inference: Identity and current role for the opening and metadata. The second book is self-published through her company's imprint, which matters when weighing launch claims.
claims.alternative: Titles and company descriptions come from her own release and from profiles built on interviews with her. A Penguin Australia listing seen in search results gives a later date for another edition; it was not opened.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck her title, company description and book list before each release and after any sale, merger or new book.

claims.claim: Own or Be Owned: Build a Business So Good It Doesn't Need You was released on September 18, 2026 under the imprint Contrarian Thinking Press, which carries her company's name.
claims.passage: which she released on September 18, 2026 through her own imprint

claims.review_trigger: Recheck the book list and any new edition or publisher before each release.

claims.claim: The book's argument, as her press release states it, is that owner dependency is a trap: a business that cannot run without its owner cannot be scaled, sold or left.
claims.passage: _Own or Be Owned_ argues that a business which cannot run without its owner is a trap.
claims.inference: Summary of the book's stated thesis from the release, needed to set up her claim that she had built the opposite.
claims.alternative: Taken from promotional copy and a magazine summary; the book itself was not read.

claims.claim: Her own statements place her birth in August 1986. In an episode published August 20, 2026 she said “I'm turning 40 this month”; PEOPLE gave her age as 39 on June 22, 2026. No source opened in this run supports a day of the month.
claims.passage: In an interview published on August 20, 2026 she said, "I'm turning 40 this month"
claims.inference: Supports a month and year only. Her statement in a mid-2024 recording that she was 37 is consistent with it.
claims.alternative: The research notes record conflicting days (August 23 and 24) on bio sites; none was verified. The recording date of the August 2026 episode is inferred from her saying she was 24 weeks pregnant, eight weeks after a 16-week post dated June 25.

claims.claim: The page's age FAQ states that she turned 40 in August 2026 and infers an August 1986 birth from her own statement plus PEOPLE's report that she was 39 on June 22, 2026; no day is given.

claims.inference: Arithmetic from two dated statements. A mid-2024 recording in which she says she is 37 is consistent.

claims.passage: She grew up in Phoenix, studied journalism at Arizona State
claims.inference: Stable background. Three 2026 profiles and her own site agree on the parents' occupations; she calls Arizona her hometown on camera.
claims.alternative: Traces to her own telling through Entrepreneur and Hispanic Executive; she calls Arizona her hometown on camera. Her parents' occupations (a father who owned a granite company, a mother who taught special education) are reported by Entrepreneur but are not stated in the draft.

Entrepreneur adds Entourage Effect Capital, which the draft does not mention. Her figures for the Latin America business vary ('a couple billion' in June 2023, 'close to a billion' in August 2023), so the draft gives none.

claims.claim: As an Arizona State journalism student she was one of 17 students whose class project on families separated by the U.S.-Mexico border, “Divided Families”, won a 2009 Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award in the college print category. The project was funded by a Howard G. Buffett Foundation grant.
claims.passage: Sanchez was one of 17 students whose class project on families separated by the U.S.-Mexico border
claims.inference: The award is real and documented by the university. It was a team award for a class project.
claims.alternative: Her own site says her coverage “earned her” the award, and her press release uses the same construction; a 2017 interviewer told her “you won” it. In her 2016 video she said “we won awards”. The accurate wording is that she shared in a team award.

claims.claim: Her own site presents the team award as hers, saying her coverage 'earned her the Robert F. Kennedy Award'.
claims.passage: Her own site says the coverage "earned her" the award
claims.inference: A documented gap between her marketing and the university's record, stated without characterizing intent.
claims.alternative: Her press release uses the same construction. In her 2016 video she said 'we won awards', and a 2017 interviewer told her 'you won' it.

claims.claim: Her account of why she left journalism has been stable since 2016: the reporting changed nothing, so she went to where power sits. In 2017: 'Right, but I thought we were going to change the world.'
claims.passage: Right, but I thought we were going to change the world
claims.inference: A ten-year-old, repeated origin story in which money is first of all power and protection, not comfort or status. It supports reading her drive as partly about leverage over outcomes.
claims.alternative: It is a polished brand narrative and the details shift: the 2016 version centers an old folks' home on the border; the 2026 versions foreground cartel violence in Juárez. The team project is documented; her individual scenes are not independently verified. The 2016 quotation is from unpunctuated captions.

claims.claim: In the 2017 interview she said the story was forgotten 'in about fifteen minutes' and that a mentor told her to 'find the centers of power. And that's money.'
claims.passage: you find the centers of power. And that's money.
claims.inference: Money appears first as leverage over outcomes, eight to nine years before the 2026 campaign versions.
claims.alternative: An advice-interview answer; the mentor is unnamed and the conversation is uncorroborated.

claims.claim: In 2026 she said the border reporting left her jaded and sent her 'where money was understood'.
claims.passage: I got jaded. So I went where money was understood.
claims.inference: The 2026 form of the origin story.
claims.alternative: Edited Q&A copy from the book campaign.

claims.claim: She describes money as protection. In 2026 she said of her border reporting that money 'decided who had protection, who had options, and who could end up dead in the desert and no one cared'.
claims.passage: It decided who had protection, who had options, and who could end up dead in the desert and no one cared.
claims.inference: First-person motive language that points at exposure to other people's will, which is the strongest thread for the Type 8 alternative.
claims.alternative: Both lines come from the 2026 book campaign, whose product is ownership as freedom, so they are also on-message marketing. The same idea appears in her 2017 interview, before the brand existed, which is why it is not dismissed.

claims.claim: She told Entrepreneur in 2026: 'If you don't have it, the world really asserts its will on you.'
claims.passage: If you don't have it, the world really asserts its will on you.
claims.inference: First-person motive language about exposure to other people's will, the root of the Type 8 alternative.
claims.alternative: A book-campaign interview whose product is ownership as freedom.

claims.claim: The origin story's central scene differs between tellings: an old folks' home on the border in her 2016 video, cartel violence in Juárez in the 2026 versions. Only the class project is independently documented.
claims.passage: Its central scene has changed with retelling
claims.inference: A comparison of her own tellings across ten years, offered as a reason to treat the story as partly brand narrative.
claims.alternative: The versions are not contradictory; a year of reporting could include both. The 2017 interview mentions elderly people left at the border and trafficking together.

claims.claim: Neither the Type 3 nor the Type 8 reading accounts well for the moral motive of her first career.
claims.passage: Neither type explains the first career well.
claims.inference: Recorded as something the type argument leaves unexplained, so the portrait is not reduced to the type.
claims.alternative: The motive is known only from her retrospective telling, which is itself a brand story.

claims.claim: She says that at Vanguard she expected a promotion and was 'told that I wasn't a team player because I never joined the happy hours'.
claims.passage: told that I wasn't a team player because I never joined the happy hours.
claims.inference: A second rejection story, told in 2026, in which the injury is being held back by gatekeepers and the vow is about never being subject to them again.
claims.alternative: Told eighteen years later to a magazine during a book launch; uncorroborated. It was not in the 2017 interview, where a different rejection story appears; they may be the same employer or different ones.

claims.claim: Her vow after that episode, as told to Entrepreneur in 2026: 'I am never going to let somebody hold me back because of my bank account.'
claims.passage: I am never going to let somebody hold me back because of my bank account.
claims.inference: A vow about never being subject to gatekeepers, which favors the control reading.
claims.alternative: Told eighteen years later during a book launch; uncorroborated.

claims.claim: In 2017 she told this story about an unnamed early employer: she proposed an international arm, was told she might run it, and hours later lost the job to someone else because, in her words, 'everyone thought I would leave dead bodies behind me to get whatever I wanted.'
claims.passage: I was told that everyone thought I would leave dead bodies behind me to get whatever I wanted.
claims.inference: The clearest early test between the two readings. Faced with a judgment that she was too ruthless, she did not reject the judges; she changed how she came across and generalized it into managing perception.
claims.alternative: One telling, eight years old, of an unnamed employer and an unnamed boss; no other party has spoken. She also took the idea elsewhere and “got the green light”, and notes the woman who got the job later joined her team, which reads as winning the contest rather than accepting the verdict.

claims.claim: Asked whether the boss had really said that, she answered: 'Yep. And maybe he was right. It was a big realization for me. I thought that I was driven, but I was putting a different message out.'
claims.passage: Yep. And maybe he was right. It was a big realization for me. I thought that I was driven, but I was putting a different message out.
claims.inference: She grants the verdict and locates the fault in the message she was sending, which is the center of the Type 3 argument.
claims.alternative: One answer in an advice interview, where presenting a lesson learned is the expected register.

claims.claim: Her response, in her words: 'I became more aware of how people perceive me. I adapted.' She adds that the woman who got the job later joined her team.
claims.passage: "I became more aware of how people perceive me. I adapted." She added a postscript: "now, the woman they gave the job to instead of me is a member of my team."
claims.inference: She changed how she came across and kept a tally of the outcome.
claims.alternative: She also says she 'got the green light somewhere else' and 'refused to let up', which reads as winning the contest as much as accepting the verdict.

claims.claim: The lesson she drew: 'I think it's about personal brand.'
claims.passage: I think it's about personal brand.
claims.inference: She generalized the episode into managing perception.
claims.alternative: In the same answer she ties it to standing out as a Latina ('Don't hide it, but be aware'), so the lesson is partly about bias she faced.

claims.claim: Faced with a judgment that she was ruthless, she treated the reputation as a fault in her own presentation rather than rejecting the judges.
claims.passage: That suggests a person who treats a bad reputation as a fault in her own presentation.
claims.inference: The draft's reading of C09, C58 and C59, marked with 'suggests'. A person organized mainly around autonomy would have more reason to reject the verdict.
claims.alternative: One telling from 2017 of an unnamed boss; no other party has spoken. A pragmatic Eight could also adapt tactically.

claims.claim: In the same 2017 interview she said, 'I just never accept the word 'no.' I hate that word.'
claims.passage: I just never accept the word 'no.' I hate that word,"
claims.inference: Shows both strands at once, before the brand: refusal of a superior's veto, and an explicit theory that being known and wanted is the route up.
claims.alternative: Advice-interview register; she is presenting herself as a model. The two statements pull toward different types and neither is decisive alone.

claims.claim: In the same interview: 'There's not a faster way to the top than to be known and wanted.'

claims.passage: I have a journal I've kept for fifteen years.

claims.claim: On her own channel in 2023: 'So I tried to figure out a way to derisk my life.'
claims.passage: So I tried to figure out a way to derisk my life.

claims.passage: I might have been more brave at twenty-one than I was at thirty.

claims.passage: because I had ownership

claims.claim: She told Hispanic Executive in 2026 that she was 'probably what every Hispanic mother and father wants for their kid' and that the career 'felt empty'.
claims.passage: I think I was probably what every Hispanic mother and father wants for their kid,

claims.claim: She says she spent years chasing goals that were not hers. Of her finance career in 2023: people who imitate others' wants 'realize they were chasing somebody else the whole time. And that's what happened to me.'
claims.passage: realize they were chasing somebody else the whole time. And that's what happened to me.
claims.inference: The strongest single line of evidence for Type 3: in three settings over three years she names the same error, shaping herself to what others reward, and treats noticing it as the turning point.
claims.alternative: Disowning borrowed ambitions is itself a popular creator narrative and she teaches 'mimetic desire' as a concept. Each statement is retrospective. Entrepreneur's paraphrase that she “spent too much time trying to follow other people's paths to success” is the reporter's wording.

claims.claim: Entrepreneur quotes her saying her parents did not understand how she could leave finance.
claims.passage: My parents didn't understand how I could leave a job like finance, a job they thought was so lucky, the best I could ever get.
claims.inference: Her parents appear as the voices urging safety, which complicates any simple story about family as the source of her nerve.
claims.alternative: Her own characterization of her parents, told during a book launch. She has also said twice that the people who love you hold you back; the draft does not use those lines.

claims.claim: On a three-day glacier climb of Mount Baker with a group of women, by her own account, she thought of herself as tougher than the others and turned back below the final ice wall. She says the real fear was 'am I like a failure by not doing this tough thing that everybody else is going to do?'
claims.passage: It was like, am I like a failure by not doing this tough thing that everybody else is going to do?
claims.inference: Asked for the moment she was most afraid, she names fear of being the one who fails in front of peers, and counts quitting as the braver act. That is failure and image, not danger or domination.
claims.alternative: A single anecdote chosen for a podcast's closing question and told as a lesson. She did defy group pressure, which an Eight could also claim.

claims.claim: On the mountain she says she realized 'most of my life I've been trying to like please a bunch of people to goals I don't care about'.
claims.passage: I just realized up here that most of my life I've been trying to like please a bunch of people to goals I don't care about.
claims.inference: With C14, the strongest line of evidence for Type 3: she names shaping herself to what others reward as her lifelong error.
claims.alternative: Disowning borrowed ambitions is a popular creator narrative and she teaches 'mimetic desire' as a concept. Retrospective.

claims.passage: I felt like it took more courage for me to not do the thing than do the thing.
claims.inference: She defied group pressure, which an Eight could also claim.
claims.alternative: A single anecdote told as a lesson.

claims.passage: Neither is the usual language of someone whose central concern is power.
claims.inference: The draft's reading of C15 and C72.
claims.alternative: One anecdote chosen for a closing question; the generalization about Type 8 language is a typological judgment.

claims.claim: She says she could only end her first marriage, a decision she calls her own, by setting a date: 'I was such a wuss I couldn't do it unless I put it on a calendar.'
claims.passage: I was such a wuss I couldn't do it unless I put it on a calendar.
claims.inference: Another self-label of fear and delay, counting against Type 8.
claims.alternative: Said while recommending deadlines as a goal-setting tool.

claims.claim: She quotes her father as a source of nerve at turning points: the 'exit tax to freedom' on leaving a marriage, and that you are not in the game until you have sat in the dark not knowing what to do.
claims.passage: there's always an exit tax to freedom.
claims.inference: A consistent detail across 2023-2026: in crises she calls her father, and she credits him with the frame that hardship is the price of freedom. It humanizes the portrait.
claims.alternative: Every quotation of the father comes through her, and the princess-or-president line comes through her and then a host's notes. Do not infer a causal childhood story; her parents also appear as the voices urging safety (C39).

claims.claim: She has said publicly that ending her first marriage was her decision and describes the period before it as a collapse of identity: 'being in the marriage was part of my identity and i didn't know how to let go of it and i felt like i was failing and there was massive shame and guilt around it'.
claims.passage: being in the marriage was part of my identity and I didn't know how to let go of it and I felt like I was failing and there was massive shame and guilt around it
claims.inference: A costly choice she narrates through failure and shame, then freedom. Useful to the type argument only as her account of herself.
claims.alternative: Her former husband is a private person who has not spoken; the draft confines itself to her statements about her own experience, names no one and adds no detail. The quotation is from unpunctuated lowercase captions of a 2022 clip; the draft capitalizes 'I' and changes nothing else. A further characterization of that marriage in the same clip is deliberately not used.

claims.claim: In an interview published September 21, 2026 she said she went to a bank to borrow against a business and was told the account she believed held about a million dollars was nearly empty; she quotes herself asking to see the screen.
claims.passage: "Excuse me, can you please turn that thing around so I can see what's on that screen?"
claims.inference: The draft's opening scene. Every detail is from her telling; her quotation of herself is reported speech.
claims.alternative: The business is unnamed and undated and no one else has told the story. It also serves as the origin story for the book's method.

claims.claim: She quotes her father's answer when she called him that night: 'If you haven't sat in the dark in the middle of the night with no idea of what to do next, you're not really in the game.'
claims.passage: If you haven't sat in the dark in the middle of the night with no idea of what to do next, you're not really in the game.
claims.inference: The father as the person she calls in a crisis. Her site attributes a differently worded version of the line to him.
claims.alternative: His words reach us only through her.

claims.passage: Like just my identity and that I was a failure because I had let an entire business fail.
claims.inference: When she is let down by a subordinate, the wound she names is failure and the fix is self-blame plus a tracking system. She does not describe confronting or punishing him. This is the 2026 instance of the pattern in C09, C15 and C16.
claims.alternative: The business is unnamed and undated and the story is uncorroborated; it also serves as the origin story for the book's method. Owners are trained to say 'it was my fault'. Her site attributes the same 'sitting in the dark' line to her father.

claims.claim: Of the manager who she says hid the shortfall: 'it was my fault for not tracking him, obviously.'
claims.passage: it was my fault for not tracking him, obviously.
claims.inference: Let down by a subordinate, she blames herself and builds a tracking system; she does not describe confronting him.
claims.alternative: Owners are trained to say 'it was my fault'. The manager is unnamed and has not given an account.

claims.claim: About twenty minutes later in the same interview, asked for her real dream, she said it began as a refusal of control: 'I don't ever want anybody to have control over me or my life again.'
claims.passage: I don't ever want anybody to have control over me or my life again.
claims.inference: The best evidence for the Type 8 alternative: an unprompted first-person statement that the early motive was never being controlled, with anger as fuel. The second half, becoming what doubters said she could not and proving herself, is achievement as vindication.
claims.alternative: One answer in one interview, reconstructed years later. 'Prove yourself' is the host's phrase. The sentence serves the book's title. 'Again' implies an earlier experience of being controlled that she does not specify.

claims.claim: She added 'I'll become every single thing that you said I wouldn't' and 'I was angry'; when Lewis Howes said 'You were trying to prove yourself', she answered 'Oh, yeah.'
claims.passage: "I'll become every single thing that you said I wouldn't,"
claims.inference: Anger as fuel favors Type 8; becoming what doubters said she could not, and proving herself, is achievement as vindication.
claims.alternative: 'Prove yourself' is the host's phrase. The quoted sentences are separated by others in the source and the draft presents them separately.

claims.claim: She says nobody will control her 'again' and has not said who did.
claims.passage: She says nobody will control her "again," and she has not said who did.
claims.inference: An unexplained element the draft declines to guess at.
claims.alternative: She may have explained it in an interview this run did not read.
claims.review_trigger: If she says publicly who or what the word 'again' refers to, report it in her words and reweigh the Type 8 alternative.

claims.claim: In 2023 she defined being rich as 'having no master. That's what rich looks like for me.'
claims.passage: having no master. That's what rich looks like for me.
claims.inference: Autonomy language three years before the 2026 statement in C28, so the theme is not new to the book. The second half is about standing and being sought out, and about not being seen to want it.
claims.alternative: The 'club' lines are an argument for content marketing. 'Thirsty' is a concern about how one appears, which fits Three better than Eight.

claims.passage: I try in my conversations with my team to almost say nothing about what my highest value is,
claims.inference: Her self-described method is selling and framing rather than command, alongside self-labels of intensity. The mix is why the typing is contested.
claims.alternative: No employee, former employee or partner has been found on record describing how she actually manages. This is the largest hole in the evidence.

claims.claim: She says owners 'try to be a dictator to our employees' or 'try to be a doormat', and that 'we don't sell enough inside of our companies'; her stated aim is to be 'so persuasive' that people act 'without them even realizing that it was your idea, not theirs'.

claims.inference: A self-label of force. In context the 'bullying' is pushing her audience and friends to act, which the draft notes.

claims.passage: not because I'm nice I'm really not that nice,

claims.alternative: Public descriptions of a marriage by one spouse, three years apart. Petkas's only on-record remarks found are on her podcast and are about fitness (S17).

claims.passage: I'm pregnant and thrilled. AND YET I've been failing at it for years.

type_hypothesis.against: Her most direct statement of motive is about control, not admiration: 'I don't ever want anybody to have control over me or my life again', with anger as the fuel (C28, C79), and it has precedents in 2017 ('I just never accept the word no', C10), 2023 ('having no master', C29) and her exits from employers over who sets the rules (C11, C57, C12, C65). She describes money as protection from other people's will (C07, C54). She walked away from the prestigious path in finance into laundromats and car washes, says she dislikes daily social media and uses it as a tool (C32), says a fan's admiration is uninteresting to her (C85), and disclaims being nice (C41). A Three is expected to move toward what earns admiration, and she repeatedly describes moving away from it. Most of the Three evidence is retrospective storytelling by a professional communicator whose audience responds to confessed failure, and no one who has worked for or against her has been found on record (C102, C43).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 8 fits a real pattern. Across a decade she frames her life as a refusal to be controlled: she left journalism for 'the centers of power' (C06, C52), treats money as what decides 'who had protection' (C07), fought the people who ran the business she built at First Trust and left when it 'wasn't my casino' (C12), stayed under two years at most jobs until she had a stake (C70), and sells a pledge that reads 'I will not do what I am told' (C50). She was told colleagues thought she would 'leave dead bodies behind' her (C09), calls herself 'the business bully' (C82) and 'really intense' (C83), jokes that a personality test labelling her something like a dictator 'sounds right' (C84), and describes her marriage as 'us against the world' (C27). Her self-sufficiency ('the one who handles it, who doesn't need help', C24) and the difficulty of asking her husband to hold her (C96) are how Eights describe vulnerability. Type 6 was considered and set aside: she names fear and de-risks carefully (C13, C68), but she shows no search for authority, allies or reassurance, and no record of doubting her own judgment. Type 7 is unlikely given 'I don't optimize for fun' (C105).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What she says was injured when a setback or a hostile judgment landed, and what she did next. An Eight's injury is being controlled, betrayed or made weak, and the response is to confront or refuse without regard to how it looks. A Three's injury is failing or being seen to fail, and the response is to adjust how she comes across, reset the score and outperform. In five separately told episodes across 2017-2026 she names failure and image and never describes a confrontation (C88): told she was too ruthless, 'maybe he was right ... I was putting a different message out', 'I became more aware of how people perceive me. I adapted', and the lesson was 'personal brand' (C09, C58, C59, C60); leaving a marriage, 'I felt like I was failing' with 'massive shame' (C16); on Mount Baker, the fear was 'am I like a failure' in front of the other women (C15); when a manager hid a business's losses, the pain was 'my identity and that I was a failure' and 'it was my fault for not tracking him' (C18, C78); of infertility, 'I've been failing at it for years' (C97). She adds two things an Eight pattern rarely volunteers: that she is a 'scaredy-cat' who staged every exit over years (C13, C68, C75), and that she spent much of her life pleasing people toward 'goals I don't care about' (C72, C14). Her self-described method with staff is persuasion, not command (C31, C81). The control statements are sincere but coincide with the product she sells (C92); the failure statements cut against the image of a self-made operator, which makes them the more diagnostic. Limit: every episode is self-told. The reading should be reversed if people who have worked for or against her describe habitual open confrontation and indifference to how she is seen (research task 2).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Why a person organized around achievement and image chose a deliberately unglamorous field and now says the visible part of her work is a chore (C32); the Three reading can call 'boring' a differentiated brand, but that is convenient. What the word 'again' refers to in 'control over me or my life again' (C80): she does not say who controlled her, and this record does not support guessing. The moral motive of her first career, reporting on separated families and trafficking, which neither type explains well (C56). How she actually treats subordinates, since her account alternates between persuasion and 'business bully' (C81, C82). Whether the confessional register of 2026 (infertility, fear, the empty bank account) is a change in her or a change in what the market rewards. And her own open question: she says she does not know what she will want after the baby arrives (C101).
